questions: Compared with iteration 1 (lead 0.03 m, same everything else), does the 0.02 m lead reduce max_error on the oval and s-bend, and does it raise progress?
Does steering_oscillation rise above the iteration-1 level of about 0.28? If so, is the cause the shorter lead or the controller response?
Where does the first off-track event occur (track, bend, progress, time)? Use per-step telemetry if available.
Does the line-loss count change, particularly on the slalom where the tape is lost on the tightest bends?
Which geometry limit now constrains the controller most: sensor lead, sensor spread, wheel_track or mass?

intent: Isolate the sensor lead. Keep the iteration-1 layout (5 sensors at x = -0.05 to +0.05 with 0.025 m spacing, 12 mm footprint, drivetrain and body unchanged) and move the sensor row from y = 0.03 m to y = 0.02 m. Expected: max_error at or below 0.06 m on the oval and s-bend, progress at or above 0.47 on the oval, and fewer off-track endings than iteration 1.
learning: Iterations 2 to 4 showed that changing the sensor footprint or the drivetrain together with other variables did not beat the iteration-1 layout. The sensor lead has never been isolated. If a 0.02 m lead improves max_error and progress, the next step is to refine the lead further or lower mass to damp oscillation. If the lead makes oscillation or line loss worse, the lead is at its useful optimum near 0.03 m and the next lever is wheel_track (between 0.09 and 0.10 m) or mass.
rationale:
Scores so far: iteration 0 = 52.3, iteration 1 = 114.4 (best), iteration 2 = 65.7, iteration 3 = 102.8, iteration 4 = 110.2. Every run in every iteration ended off track with zero finishes. Max error sits at 0.061 to 0.068 m against an off-track limit of max(0.06, 0.0125 + body_width/4) = 0.06 m, while RMS error stays at 0.023 to 0.031 m. The robot tracks well until a single excursion carries it past the edge, so the lever is the response to excursions, not general tracking. Body width cannot help: even at 0.18 m the limit is 0.0575 m, so the 0.06 m floor governs.

Sensor array tests: 7 sensors at 16 mm cut oval progress to 0.23, and 5 sensors at 8 mm gave 0.41. The 5-sensor, 12 mm array of iteration 1 remains the best sensor layout. Drivetrain tests: iteration 4 (wheel_radius 0.04, mass 0.5, body_length 0.12) did not beat iteration 1. Oval progress was 0.46 vs 0.47, max_error rose to 0.068, and steering oscillation rose from 0.28 to 0.33. So the lighter, faster drivetrain overshoots as much as it gains.

What has not been isolated is the sensor lead. Iteration 0 used 0.05 m and iteration 1 used 0.03 m, but each change was made together with other changes. A lead of 0.03 m puts the sensors just ahead of the axle, so they see the line late on bends. I therefore return to the iteration-1 design, which is the best measured, and change only the sensor lead, from 0.03 m to 0.02 m. This is a single-variable test. The sensors move closer to the axle, which shortens the sensing-to-wheel delay on tight bends and should cut the excursion at the edge. The drivetrain stays at iteration 1 values (wheel_radius 0.035, wheel_track 0.10, mass 0.6, body_length 0.14), so any change in max_error or progress can be attributed to the lead.

Expected result: oval progress at or above 0.47, max_error reduced toward or below 0.06 m, and fewer off-track endings than iteration 1. Risk: a lead of 0.02 m may reduce the look-ahead too far, so the signal reacts too late and steering oscillation rises.
